What is the relationship between size and distance in terms of visual acuity?
Write briefly about visual acuity?
answer: 2. The key relationship can be summarized as:
Visual angle (θ) = arctan (object size / viewing distance)
• As distance increases, the visual angle decreases, making the object appear smaller and harder to resolve.
• Conversely, increasing the size of an object at the same distance increases its visual angle, improving visibility.

3. Visual acuity is the medical term for sharpness of vision. It is defined as the power of the eye to see a smallest object or letter clearly and distinguishably at specified distances. It is the ability of the eye to resolve fine details. It is influenced by the size of an object and its distance from the observer, which together determine the visual angle.

prompts: What is your diagnosis?
What are some causes of this condition?
answer: Note: This condition may lead certain glaucoma types. Glaucoma Types Associated with Posterior Synechiae:

Mechanism: Extensive posterior synechiae can cause pupillary block, preventing aqueous humor from flowing through the pupil, leading to increased posterior chamber pressure, anterior bowing of the iris (iris bombé), and subsequent angle closure.
Common Causes: Uveitis (chronic or recurrent), trauma, post-surgical inflammation.
Mechanism: Chronic uveitis leads to inflammation, synechiae formation, and trabecular meshwork dysfunction, causing IOP elevation.
Common Causes: Chronic anterior uveitis (e.g., juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Fuchs’ heterochromic iridocyclitis).

Mechanism: Ischemia-induced neovascularization (from conditions like diabetic retinopathy or central retinal vein occlusion) can promote posterior synechiae formation, contributing to both pupillary block and angle closure.
Mechanism: If posterior synechiae cause prolonged lens-induced inflammation, the lens can become swollen (intumescent cataract), leading to angle narrowing and IOP elevation.

cards.stem: A mechanic was rushed to the Accident and Emergency room as a result of a chemical spillage into his eye while working on a faulty car.
prompts: How would you manage this patient?
answer: 1. Let the patient lie supine on a bed.
2. Expose face and eye (in case there is a covering).
3. Use 3 litres of Ringer’s lactate (Hartmann’s solution) to rinse the eye thoroughly.

Note: In case there is no Ringer’s lactate available, use Normal Saline. If Normal saline is not available, use lukewarm water. If lukewarm water is also not available, use any available fluid such as urine, etc.

4. When irrigating or rinsing the eye, do not fetch the fluid with a cup or any container and flush the eye with it. Rather, hang the Ringer’s lactate or the fluid on an IV drip stand and release the bevel of the IV line to drip continuously on the eye to rinse it.
5. Use a litmus paper (if available) on the affected eye to check for the pH of the fluid that spilled on it - to determine whether it was acidic or basic.

6. Administer IV lidocaine onto the affected eye in other reduce pain and hypersensitivity of the eye. If lidocaine eye drops are available (while the IV lidocaine is not available), administer that instead.
7. Use a cotton bud or a sterile gauze to swap the fornices of the eye.
8. Monitor the patient at regular time interval and refer to an Ophthalmologist for further assessment and management.

cards.subject: ophthalmology
prompts: Describe the findings in this image.
What is your impression / most likely diagnosis?
answer: 1. Optic Disc: The optic disc appears bright, which could be due to the lighting in the image rather than pathological cupping or pallor.
2. Retinal Vessels: The blood vessels appear somewhat tortuous, but no obvious signs of arteriovenous nicking, hemorrhages, or neovascularization are clearly visible.
3. Macula: There is a darker spot in the macular area, which might indicate a pathological change such as macular edema, hemorrhage, or a pigmentary alteration.
4. Peripheral Retina: There seems to be a small marked area (green star) in the superior retina, possibly indicating a lesion or an area of interest.
• The darker lesion in the macula could suggest diabetic macular edema (DME) or an early stage of age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
• If this image represents a hypertensive or diabetic retinopathy model, other changes (microaneurysms, cotton wool spots, or hemorrhages) might be expected.
refs: 1. Diabetic Retinopathy: Wilkinson CP, Ferris FL, Klein RE, et al. Proposed international clinical diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema disease severity scales. Ophthalmology. 2003;110(9):1677-1682. doi:10.1016/S01616420(03)00475-5.
2. Hypertensive Retinopathy: Wong TY, Mitchell P. Hypertensive retinopathy. N Engl J Med. 2004;351(22):2310-2317. doi:10.1056/NEJMra032865.
3. Age-Related Macular Degeneration: Jager RD, Mieler WF, Miller JW. Age related macular degeneration. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(24):2606-2617. doi:10.1056/NEJMra0801537.

cards.subject: ophthalmology
prompts: Describe the findings in this image.
What is your impression / most likely diagnosis?
answer: This retinal image appears to show multiple yellow-white exudates (hard exudates), hemorrhages, and possible areas of retinal edema, which are characteristic of diabetic retinopathy, likely proliferative or severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR).
• These are yellowish-white deposits of lipids and proteins that result from chronic vascular leakage.
• Typically seen in diabetic maculopathy and can threaten central vision.
• Multiple dark hemorrhages scattered across the retina, indicating vascular damage and microaneurysms.
• Common in diabetic retinopathy and hypertensive retinopathy.
• Some pale, ill-defined areas may represent retinal ischemia due to microvascular occlusion.
• The optic disc appears normal, but the blood vessels show some dilation and tortuosity, which can be associated with vascular pathology.
This image strongly suggests diabetic retinopathy (likely severe NPDR or early proliferative DR).
• Severe NPDR: If neovascularization is absent but features such as extensive hemorrhages and venous beading are present.
• Proliferative DR (PDR): If neovascularization is seen (not clearly visible here, but could be present).
1. Hypertensive Retinopathy (if associated with arteriolar narrowing and cotton wool spots).
2. Retinal Vein Occlusion (if hemorrhages are more widespread and associated with significant venous engorgement).
refs: 1. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach (9th Edition) – Brad Bowling. Chapter: Diabetic Retinopathy, Pages: 517-524.
2. Vaughan & Asbury's General Ophthalmology (19th Edition) – Paul Riordan-Eva, John P. Whitcher. Chapter 14: Retinal Vascular Disease, Pages: 212-218.
3. American Academy of Ophthalmology: Basic and Clinical Science Course (BCSC), Section 12 – Retina and Vitreous. Chapter: Diabetic Retinopathy, Pages: 98-110.

cards.subject: ophthalmology
prompts: Describe the findings in this image.
What is your impression / most likely diagnosis?
answer: This retinal image appears relatively normal at first glance, but subtle abnormalities suggest possible optic disc swelling and macular involvement, which may indicate optic disc edema or papilledema.
• The optic disc appears blurred and swollen, particularly at the margins.
• This suggests increased intracranial pressure (papilledema) or local optic nerve pathology (optic neuritis).
• The foveal reflex is somewhat dull, and there appears to be a subtle reddish hue in the macular region, which could indicate early macular edema or inflammation.
• No obvious microaneurysms, hemorrhages, or neovascularization are seen, ruling out diabetic retinopathy.
• The veins appear slightly congested, which may be a sign of increased intracranial pressure.
• If this is bilateral, it strongly suggests increased intracranial pressure due to conditions such as a brain tumor, idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), or hydrocephalus.
• If associated with vision loss and pain on eye movement, this could indicate optic neuritis, seen in multiple sclerosis (MS).
• If associated with systemic hypertension, this could be a sign of malignant hypertension leading to optic disc edema.
• Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) – If venous congestion is more pronounced.
• Diabetic Papillopathy – If the patient has diabetes with mild disc swelling.
• Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION) – If seen in older patients with sudden vision loss.
refs: 1. Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach (9th Edition) – Brad Bowling. Chapter: The Optic Nerve and Visual Pathway, Pages: 776-780 (Papilledema).
2. Vaughan & Asbury's General Ophthalmology (19th Edition) – Paul Riordan-Eva, John P. Whitcher. Chapter: Optic Neuropathies, Pages: 245-250.
3. American Academy of Ophthalmology: Basic and Clinical Science Course (BCSC), Section 5 – Neuro-Ophthalmology. Chapter: Papilledema and Optic Neuropathies,
Pages: 72-80.

notes.title: Ophthalmology Funduscopy
lines: It is used for fundus examination and to observe any abnormality of the ocular media.
1. Ensure dim light in the examination room (if the light is on, humbly request to put it off !!!!!).
2. Have patient to remove their glasses (if they have them on), you may be required to do same if you use glasses.
3. Remember!!! Always assess Right eye with Right hand (R-R) and Left eye with Left hand (L-L), hand on patient’s forehead.
4. Have patient look at distant point, direct light about 12 inches away at 15 degree angle.
5. Note the Red reflex (reflection of retina) - Present and Bright/Dull or Absent.
• For a normal eye, it should be yellow (yellow) to pink/red, round or oval with distinct margins.
• If pale it could mean partial death of nerve.
• If edematous, blurred margins (papilledema) could mean increased Intraocular pressure (IOP).
• Check for Cup-to-Disc Ratio (CDR): Normal is 0. 0 to 0. 5, Abnormal is 0. 6 - 1. 0
7. Note branching of vessels from the disc.
• It should branch out and become smaller as move distally.
• Found temporally or laterally (in trying to see, it may cause watering of patient’s eye).
Note that: A Normal fundus will have;
1. Pink optic disc with cup in the centre.
2. Arteries lighter in colour and narrower than veins.
3. Red background due to choroidal vessels and retinal pigment epithelium.
